Variant constraint: No distillation of reusable directions from prior top-ranked

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

TitleCross-lingual Subnet Distillation: Efficient Adaptation of Multilingual NMT
via Lightweight Adapter Routing for Extreme Low-Resource Languages

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemMultilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) models such as M2M-100 and
NLLB cover hundreds of language pairs but degrade sharply on extreme
low-resource languages (training corpus <100K sentence pairs). Two common
approaches — full fine-tuning and language-family adapter modules — suffer from
either catastrophic forgetting of high-resource languages or parameter
inefficiency when scaling to dozens of low-resource pairs. Existing
adapter-based methods typically assign one adapter per language or per language
pair, which does not exploit cross-lingual transfer between typologically
related low-resource languages that share structural patterns. The core problem
is: how can we share a small set of adapter parameters across related
low-resource languages without hand-crafted language groupings or prior
knowledge about which languages benefit from sharing?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA shared pool of lightweight adapter modules combined with a learned
routing mechanism can automatically discover beneficial parameter-sharing
patterns among extreme low-resource languages. Specifically:

 • A small set of cross-lingual subnets (e.g.,4–8 adapter modules per
   Transformer layer) is sufficient to cover the syntactic and morphological
   variation across a diverse set of low-resource languages.
 • A gating network trained jointly with the adapters can route each language's
   hidden states through the appropriate subnets, enabling positive transfer
   while preventing interference.
 • This approach yields BLEU/COMET gains of ≥2.0 points over per-language
   adapters and ≥1.5 points over language-family adapters on the lowest-resource
   quartile of FLORES-200, with <5% additional parameters over the base MNMT
   model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodThree-stage pipeline:

 1 Base model & frozen backbone. Start from a pretrained MNMT encoder-decoder
   (e.g., NLLB-600M). Freeze all backbone parameters. Insert a small set of K
   learnable adapter subnets per Transformer layer (each subnet =
   down-projection → ReLU → up-projection, bottleneck dimension d =64). This
   follows the standard bottleneck adapter architecture (Houlsby et al.,2019)
   but with multiple independent copies per layer.
 2 Learned router. For each language l in the set of target low-resource
   languages, a lightweight gating network takes the hidden state h at each
   layer and outputs a soft distribution over the K subnets:

 • Router = single linear layer with softmax: g(h) = softmax(W_r · h), output
   dimension K.
 • The final adapter output is the weighted combination of all K subnets: Σ_k
   g_k(h) · subnet_k(h).
 • Router parameters are shared across all low-resource languages but
   conditioned on the current language via a learned language embedding.

 3 Training. Train adapters + router jointly on a curated set of ~20 extreme
   low-resource languages (each with5K–100K sentence pairs). Use a
   temperature-annealed version of the routing softmax to encourage
   specialization over time. Include a small auxiliary loss that penalizes
   entropy of the routing distribution to incentivize each language to select a
   compact subset of subnets.

During inference for a held-out low-resource language, the router automatically
selects the appropriate mixture of subnets without any manual grouping.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A subset of the FLORES-200 dataset covering20
extreme low-resource languages (e.g., Acehnese, Balinese, Bambara, Central
Kurdish, Crimean Tatar, Dholuo, Eastern Mari, Fijian, Guarani, Ilocano, Kamba,
Kashmiri, Kikuyu, Kinyarwanda, Kyrgyz, Lombard, Madurese, Maori, Minangkabau,
Nuer), paired with English. Each pair has between5K and100K parallel sentences
from the NLLB corpus.

 • Evaluation: FLORES-200 devtest for the same20 languages (translation into
   English and from English). Primary: spBLEU (sacrébleu tokenized) and COMET-22
   (wmt22-comet-da). Secondary: chrF++.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | spBLEU | Standard lexical overlap; primary for direct comparison
with NLLB baselines | | COMET-22 | Learned metric that captures semantic
adequacy; less biased toward high-resource languages | | chrF++ |
Character-level n-gram overlap; informative for morphologically rich
low-resource languages | | Router entropy (per language) | Diagnostic: does each
language converge to a distinct routing pattern or collapse to uniform? | | Avg.
# active subnets per language | Measures parameter efficiency and degree of
specialization | | BLEU on high-resource languages (e.g., French, Chinese) |
Check for catastrophic forgetting on languages seen during MNMT pretraining |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. NLLB-600M (frozen backbone + no adapters): Zero-shot baseline —
simply evaluate the pretrained model without any additional training. Measures
the gap this proposal aims to close.

 2 Per-language adapters (NLLB +1 adapter/lang): One dedicated bottleneck
   adapter per low-resource language, no sharing. Upper bound on parameter
   count; lower bound on cross-lingual transfer.
 3 Language-family adapters (grouped by NLLB taxonomy): One adapter per
   predefined language family (e.g., Austronesian, Niger-Congo, Turkic).
   Represents the best static-grouping baseline.
 4 Full fine-tuning of NLLB on the20-language corpus: Upper bound on
   per-language performance but at high forgetting risk. Included to quantify
   the forgetting-adaptation trade-off.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What it tests |

|---|---| | K =2,4,8,16 | Sensitivity to number of subnets; what is the minimal
K needed? | | Without auxiliary entropy penalty | Does the entropy
regularization actually encourage specialization, or is soft routing sufficient
alone? | | Shared router vs. per-language router | Is conditioning on language
embeddings in the router necessary, or can a single router handle all20
languages? | | Bottleneck d =32 vs.64 vs.128 | Trade-off between parameter
efficiency and capacity | | Temperature annealing schedule | Does hard vs. soft
routing make a difference? | | Random routing (fixed random gating) | Are
learned routing patterns better than random assignment? Controls for the benefit
of learning. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Collapse to uniform routing. If the router assigns
equal weight to all subnets for every language, the method degenerates into a
single larger adapter. Mitigation: the entropy penalty explicitly penalizes
this; monitor router entropy as a diagnostic.

 2 Low-resource languages too dissimilar. If the20 languages are so
   typologically diverse that no beneficial sharing exists, per-language
   adapters may outperform the shared-pool approach. Mitigation: stratify the
   language set to include at least two pairs of closely related languages
   (e.g., Madurese/Indonesian, Kikuyu/Kamba) to maximize chance of detectable
   transfer.
 3 Instability in routing during early training. Random initial routing may
   cause noisy gradients that prevent convergence. Mitigation: use a warmup
   phase where routing is uniform (temperature high), then anneal.
 4 Catastrophic forgetting of high-resource languages. Even with a frozen
   backbone, adapter outputs may drift. Mitigation: evaluate BLEU on French and
   Chinese after training; if drop exceeds0.5 BLEU, add a small replay buffer of
   high-resource pairs.
 5 Marginal gains on very small datasets (<10K pairs). With extremely limited
   data, even parameter sharing may not help; the bottleneck dimension may be
   too large relative to the training signal. Mitigation: include a baseline
   with d =32 and consider whether pretrained word-level alignments (e.g.,
   LASER) could augment the signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations1. English-centric. Both training and evaluation are
English⇄low-resource. The method's generality to low-resource⇄low-resource
translation is untested.

 2 Bottleneck adapter capacity. Adapters are fundamentally low-rank
   approximations; for morphologically complex languages, a rank-64 bottleneck
   may underspecify certain inflectional phenomena. Character-level or
   morpheme-level decoding is not explored here.
 3 Router training cost. Jointly training the gating network introduces
   additional training overhead (~1.5× per-step cost vs. per-language adapters)
   and may require careful hyperparameter tuning across20 languages
   simultaneously.
 4 No explicit orthographic or phonological features. The router conditions only
   on pretrained language embeddings, not on typological features (e.g., word
   order, case marking) that could guide sharing. This is a deliberate design
   choice to avoid human priors, but it may leave gains on the table.
 5 Single backbone scale (600M parameters). Whether the findings transfer to
   larger (3.3B) or smaller (300M) backbones is unknown. The optimal K and d
   likely scale with model capacity.
 6 No iterative back-translation or monolingual data. The proposal uses only
   parallel data. Incorporating monolingual data (back-translation,
   self-training) is a natural extension but is outside the scope of this
   method's core contribution.

Research Proposal: Cross-Lingual Contrastive Retrieval for Low-Resource Neural
Machine Translation## Title
CREST-MT: Cross-Lingual Contrastive
Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Machine Translation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Neural machine translation (NMT) for low-resource language pairs suffers
from data sparsity. While massively multilingual pretrained models (e.g., mBART,
NLLB) provide a strong foundation, they are expensive to deploy and fine-tune,
and their coverage of truly low-resource languages remains uneven. Current
approaches either rely on large-scale back-translation (which introduces noise)
or on pivoting through a high-resource language (which compounds errors). There
is no established method that efficiently selects high-quality synthetic
training data from monolingual corpora without requiring a seed translation
system or a large teacher model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Cross-lingual sentence embeddings, learned via a lightweight
contrastive objective on a small bilingual dictionary (≤5k entries), can
retrieve high-quality parallel sentence pairs from monolingual corpora to
augment a small seed parallel corpus. An NMT model fine-tuned on this augmented
data will outperform: (1) training on the seed corpus alone, (2) standard
back-translation augmentation, and (3) using generic multilingual sentence
encoders (e.g., LaBSE) for retrieval, particularly when the total compute budget
is ≤1 GPU-day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Retriever1. Input:5,000 word-level
translation pairs from a bilingual dictionary (or automatically induced via
unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction). Two large monolingual corpora (source
side: ~5M sentences, target side: ~5M sentences).

2 Encoder: A small dual-encoder Transformer (2 layers,256-dim hidden,4 heads —
≈6M parameters) initialized independently on source and target monolingual
data via masked language modeling (1 epoch each).
3 Contrastive alignment: For each dictionary entry, sample an equal number of
unrelated source/target words as negatives. Optimize with InfoNCE loss + a
margin of0.3. No back-translation or parallel data is needed.
4 Retrieval: Encode all sentences from both monolingual corpora with the
aligned encoder. For each source sentence, retrieve the top-5 target
sentences by cosine similarity. Apply a confidence threshold (≥0.7) to retain
only high-confidence pairs.

Stage2: NMT Fine-Tuning1. Seed parallel corpus:20k sentence pairs.

2 Augmented corpus: Seed + high-confidence retrieved pairs (expected
yield:50k–150k depending on language pair — accept50k as minimum).
3 Model:6-layer Transformer (512-dim,8-head encoder-decoder) — intentionally
kept small.
4 Training: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy (label smoothing ε=0.1), Adam
(β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98), inverse sqrt learning rate scheduler (warmup4000 steps).
Batch size4096 tokens. Early stopping based on dev perplexity (patience5).1
GPU-day budget on a single A100.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Size | Source |

|---|---|---| | Bilingual dictionary |5,000 pairs | Wiktionary / PanLex /
automatic induction | | Seed parallel (train) |20k pairs | JW300 or Tatoeba | |
Monolingual (source) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | |
Monolingual (target) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | | Dev |2k
pairs | FLORES-200 dev split | | Test |2k pairs | FLORES-200 devtest split |

Language pair: Gujarati → English (gu-en), a genuinely low-resource pair with
under100k publicly available parallel sentences. The same pipeline should also
be evaluated on a second pair (e.g., Kazakh → English) to ensure results are not
language-specific.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- BLEU (sacrébleu signature:
nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp) — primary metric- chrF++
(character-level) — secondary, captures morphologically faithful translations-
COMET (wmt22-comet-da) — neural metric for semantic adequacy- Retrieval
precision@1 on held-out bilingual dictionary entries (to validate the retriever
quality in Stage1)

• Effective augmentation yield: number of retrieved pairs above the confidence
thresholdAll NMT models are run with 3 random seeds. We report means with95%
bootstrap confidence intervals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| # | Method | Key Difference from CREST-MT |

|---|---|---| | B1 | Seed-only fine-tuning | No data augmentation | | B2 | Seed
+ standard back-translation | Uses a target→source model to back-translate
target monolingual data | | B3 | Seed + LaBSE-based retrieval (Feng et al.,2022)
| Replaces our contrastive retriever with the publicly available LaBSE encoder |
| B4 | mBART-50 fine-tuned on seed (4 layers unfrozen) | Multilingual pretrained
baseline,4× parameter cost | | B5 | Random retrieval: seed + randomly paired
monolingual sentences | Upper bound on noise; controls for data quantity alone |
| B6 | Bilingual dictionary induction baseline: replaces the dictionary with an
automatically induced one (unsupervised) | Tests sensitivity to dictionary
quality |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Retriever size: Remove contrastive alignment entirely (train on
word-level MLM only, no bilingual signal).

2 Confidence threshold: Vary the threshold (0.5,0.7,0.85,0.95) to measure
precision–recall trade-off on retrieved pairs.
3 Dictionary size: Reduce dictionary from5k →1k →200 entries to measure how
much bilingual signal the retriever needs.
4 Negative sampling strategy: Compare random negatives vs. in-batch negatives
vs. hard negative mining via TF-IDF similarity.
5 Monolingual data quantity: Subset source/target monolingual data from5M →500k
→50k sentences.
6 NMT model scale: Increase NMT to12-layer/1024-dim to test whether gains
persist in larger models.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|---|---|---| | Retriever yields no high-confidence pairs (<50k) | Medium —
depends on how well dictionary covers the monolingual data | Fall back to a
weaker threshold (0.5) and filter by round-trip consistency instead; if still
<50k, report ablation (A2) to characterize the threshold boundary | | Augmented
data is too noisy and degrades BLEU | Low–Medium — random retrieval baseline
(B5) bounds noise, and contrastive retrieval should be better than random |
Measure per-pair confidence and stratify test-set BLEU by retrieval confidence
quartiles; if low-confidence pairs actively hurt, use confidence-weighted
training loss | | Dictionary quality is poor (many incorrect entries) | Low for
Wiktionary; Medium for automatically induced dictionaries | B6 ablation tests
this explicitly; if Wiktionary exists for the language pair, use it; if not,
report the induction baseline separately | | Gains appear only on small NMT
model, vanish at scale | Medium — larger models have stronger language priors
and may not benefit from extra data | Ablation A6 tests this directly; if gains
vanish, reframe contribution as "efficient retrieval for small models" | |
Computational budget (1 GPU-day) is insufficient | Low — the small encoder and
modest NMT are designed to fit this budget | Profile training step time; if
close to the limit, reduce monolingual data to2M sentences and cap NMT epochs
at30 | | Results are language-pair specific | Medium — gu-en may be easy due to
shared script in some domains, or hard due to limited data quality | Replicate
on a second language pair (kk-en) with distinct script and different data
sources; report both in the main paper |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Research Proposal: Structure-Aware Neural Program Repair via Differentiable
Graph-Based Code Representations## ProblemAutomated program repair (APR) aims to
reduce the human cost of debugging by generating patches for buggy code. Current
   state-of-the-art neural APR systems fall into two camps with complementary
 weaknesses. LLM-based approaches (e.g., fine-tuned Codex, CodeT5, or prompted
  GPT-4) treat code as flat text or token sequences. They can generate fluent
  patches but frequently produce syntactically invalid or semantically shallow
fixes — renaming variables, adding trivially correct lines, or hallucinating API
 calls that do not exist — because they have no explicit representation of the
   program's syntactic or data-flow structure. Syntax-aware approaches (e.g.,
  tree-based RNNs, graph neural networks over ASTs) incorporate structure but
  operate on fixed, hand-engineered graph schemas (typically just the abstract
   syntax tree) that miss cross-procedure data-flow and control dependencies,
   limiting their ability to fix bugs that span multiple functions or require
                              data-flow reasoning.

The core problem is that neither approach jointly models syntactic
well-formedness (ensuring the patch parses and type-checks) with semantic
relevance (ensuring the patch actually changes program behavior in the intended
way). Patches that are syntactically valid but semantically vacuous inflate
repair rates on benchmarks without actually fixing bugs, while structurally
grounded models fail on bugs requiring information flow beyond the local AST
neighborhood.

HypothesisExplicitly injecting a differentiable, multi-relational program graph
— combining abstract syntax tree edges, data-flow edges (def-use chains),
control-flow edges, and call-graph edges — into a transformer-based
encoder-decoder architecture for APR will yield higher semantically correct
repair rates compared to both text-only LLM fine-tuning and single-relational
(AST-only) graph approaches. Specifically, the multi-relational graph structure
provides two advantages: (1) it grounds patch generation in syntactic
well-formedness by preserving the AST backbone, and (2) it enables the model to
attend to non-local information flow (e.g., "this variable is used50 lines below
in a different function") that flat attention cannot efficiently capture. The
critical sub-hypothesis is that data-flow edges contribute more to semantic
correctness than AST edges for multi-statement and cross-procedure bugs, while
AST edges matter more for single-statement local fixes.

MethodWe propose RepairGNN, a structure-aware neural program repair system built
on a transformer backbone augmented with relational graph convolution over a
multi-relational program graph.

Program Graph Construction. Given a buggy program, we parse it into a joint
graph (G = (V, E_1, E_2, E_3, E_4)) where:

 • Nodes (V): AST tokens (terminals) and intermediate non-terminal nodes, plus
   additional statement-level and function-level nodes.
 • Edges (E_1) (AST edges): parent-child relationships from the parse tree.
 • Edges (E_2) (data-flow edges): def-use chains connecting variable definitions
   to their uses, extracted via static analysis.
 • Edges (E_3) (control-flow edges): successor-predecessor relations between
   basic blocks.
 • Edges (E_4) (call edges): caller-callee relationships between functions.

Architecture. The model is an encoder-decoder transformer. The encoder processes
the buggy program as a token sequence augmented with relational graph biases:

 1 Token embedding layer — each node's token is embedded via a learned lookup.
 2 Relational graph encoder — a stack of (L) transformer layers, each
   interleaved with a Relational Graph Attention sub-layer. In this sub-layer,
   the attention logit from token (i) to token (j) is modulated by a learned
   bias (b_{r(i,j)}) that depends on the relation type (AST parent, AST child,
   def-use, control-flow successor/predecessor, call, or no relation). This is
   similar to Graph Attention Networks but with typed edges where each relation
   type has its own learned bias and optionally a separate transformation
   matrix.
 3 Decoder — a standard autoregressive transformer that attends to encoder
   outputs and generates the patch token-by-token, constrained by a beam search
   that filters candidates failing to parse or type-check.

Training. Two-stage training:

 • Stage1 (pre-training): Masked language modeling objective on a large corpus
   of code (e.g., The Stack or CodeSearchNet) with the relational graph encoder,
   learning to reconstruct masked tokens.
 • Stage2 (fine-tuning): Standard sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning on
   buggy-fixed program pairs. Loss is cross-entropy over patch tokens.

Inference. Beam search with width (k=10). Candidates are filtered by a
validation oracle (syntax check, type check, and test execution if available).
The final candidate is selected by a confidence score from the model re-ranked
by a small trained verifier that scores patch plausibility based on edit
distance and structural validity.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on three standard benchmarks for APR:

 • Defects4J (v2.0):835 real Java bugs from17 open-source projects. The standard
   benchmark for APR evaluation. We report both plausible (passes all tests) and
   correct (semantically equivalent to ground-truth patch, verified by manual
   inspection or differential testing) patch rates.
 • HumanEval-Java: The HumanEval benchmark ported to Java by Google Research.164
   hand-written programming problems with test cases. We construct buggy
   versions using automated mutation (single-statement and multi-statement
   mutants), providing a controlled setting where the ground-truth fix is known.
 • QuixBugs (Java subset):40 buggy programs translated from QuixBugs. Each has a
   single-bug, single-fix structure. Useful for analyzing local vs. non-local
   repair performance.

For cross-language generalization, we additionally evaluate on:

 • BugsInPy:154 real bugs from15 Python projects, to test whether the graph
   construction generalizes to Python's dynamic type system.

All experiments use5 random seeds and report mean and95% confidence intervals
across seeds.

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary? |

|--------|-----------|----------| | Correct Repair Rate (CRR) | Fraction of bugs
for which the generated patch is semantically equivalent to the developer fix
(Defects4J manual annotation) or passes all tests (HumanEval-Java). | Yes | |
Plausible Repair Rate (PRR) | Fraction of bugs for which the patch passes all
available tests (may be overfitted or incorrect). | Secondary | | Syntactic
Validity Rate (SVR) | Fraction of generated patches that parse without syntax
errors. | Diagnostic | | Edit Distance (ED) | Average Levenshtein distance
between generated and ground-truth patches (only for bugs with known fixes). |
Diagnostic | | Type-Safety Rate (TSR) | Fraction of patches that pass
type-checking (Java only). | Diagnostic | | Top-(k) Accuracy | Whether the
correct patch is within the top-(k) beam candidates. | Analysis |

Primary metric is CRR. PRR alone is misleading (high plausible but low correct
rates are common in APR). SVR and TSR isolate syntactic vs. semantic failures.

BaselinesWe compare against eight baselines spanning the main paradigms in
neural APR:


 Baseline                  Category                   Key Features
 CodeT5-base (fine-tuned)  Text-only encoder-decoder  Flat token sequence, no
                                                      explicit structure
 CodeBERT + seq2seq        Text-only encoder + LSTM   Pre-trained code-aware
                           decoder                    embeddings, no structural
                                                      bias
 Recoder                   Syntax-guided editing      Places buggy tokens into
                                                      a placeholder template;
                                                      uses AST paths for
                                                      editing
 DEAR                      AST-based graph            Tree-based LSTM over AST;
                                                      single relation type
                                                      (parent-child)
 Hoppity (DLFix)           Edit-sequence prediction   Predicts edit operations
                                                      (delete, insert, replace)
                                                      at token level
 SelfAPR (GPT-3.5)         LLM prompting              Few-shot prompt with
                                                      buggy code, no
                                                      fine-tuning, no
                                                      structural bias
 RepairLLaMA (fine-tuned)  Text-only decoder          Fine-tuned Code LLaMA on
                                                      bug-fix pairs
 CURE                      Code-aware pre-training +  Pre-trains on code with
                           APR fine-tuning            syntax-aware objectives,
                                                      but no explicit graph
                                                      during fine-tuning


All baselines are evaluated on identical train/validation/test splits. To ensure
fair comparison, we use the same tokenizer and vocabulary as CodeT5 for all
learned models.

AblationsWe design ablations to isolate the contribution of each component,
mirroring the Table3 structure:

Ablation1: Graph Relation Types| Variant | Relations Used | Expected Impact |

|---------|---------------|----------------| | Full RepairGNN | AST + Data-flow
+ Control-flow + Call | — | | − Data-flow | AST + Control-flow + Call | CRR drop
on multi-statement bugs | | − Control-flow | AST + Data-flow + Call | Modest
drop, mostly on ordering-sensitive patches | | − Call | AST + Data-flow +
Control-flow | Small drop, mostly on cross-function bugs | | − AST | Data-flow +
Control-flow + Call | Large CRR drop, many syntactically invalid patches | |
AST-only | AST edges only | Matches DEAR-like approach; gap to full reveals
value of non-local edges |

Ablation2: Training Objectives| Variant | Pre-training | Fine-tuning | Expected
Impact |

|---------|-------------|-------------|----------------| | Full | MLM + graph
structure | Seq2seq with graph | — | | − Pre-train | None | Seq2seq with graph |
CRR drop on rare bug patterns | | − Graph in fine-tune | MLM + graph | Seq2seq
flat (no graph bias) | Tests whether graph helps at inference or only during
representation learning |

Ablation3: Relational Attention vs. Alternatives| Variant | Structural
Integration | Expected Impact |

|---------|----------------------|----------------| | Full (RelGraphAttn) |
Learnable per-relation bias in self-attention | — | | Graph-as-Sequence |
Flatten graph into a linearized token sequence with special tokens for edges |
Worse than RelGraphAttn due to loss of structural inductive bias | | GNN-Only
(no transformer) | Relational GCN encoder + LSTM decoder | Worse due to limited
receptive field |

Ablation4: Inference Strategy| Variant | Post-hoc Filtering | Expected Impact |

|---------|-------------------|----------------| | Full | Syntax + type +
confidence re-ranking | — | | No filtering | Raw beam search output | TSR and
SVR drop significantly | | Oracle filtering | Use ground-truth tests (if
available) as filter | Upper bound on achievable CRR |

Expected Failure Modes1. Graph construction quality for real-world bugs.
Defects4J bugs can span multiple files. Our graph currently models single-file
programs. For multi-file bugs, the graph will miss cross-file data-flow and call
edges, reducing repair accuracy. Mitigation: flag and report multi-file bugs as
a separate analysis category rather than silently including them.

 2 Graph sparsity for short programs. For single-line bugs in small functions
   (common in QuixBugs), the multi-relational graph adds little information over
   the AST alone, so RepairGNN may not outperform simpler AST-only baselines on
   these cases. Mitigation: stratified analysis by bug complexity
   (single-statement vs. multi-statement vs. cross-procedure).
 3 Overfitting to dataset-specific patterns. Defects4J has a well-known bias
   toward certain bug types (null pointer, off-by-one, incorrect condition). If
   the model learns to exploit these patterns rather than actually reasoning
   about structure, performance on out-of-distribution bugs will be low.
   Mitigation: cross-benchmark evaluation (Defects4J → HumanEval-Java transfer)
   and addition of manually crafted out-of-distribution bug test cases.
 4 Training instability with multi-relational attention. Adding multiple
   relation-specific bias terms increases the number of learned parameters in
   the attention mechanism. If not properly regularized, the relational biases
   may collapse (all relations learn the same bias), rendering the graph
   structure inert. Mitigation: add an auxiliary loss that enforces divergence
   between relation-bias distributions (pairwise KL divergence between relation
   attention patterns).
 5 Beam search bias toward short patches. Standard beam search favors shorter
   sequences due to length-normalization effects, causing the model to produce
   incomplete or trivially minimal patches. Mitigation: use length normalization
   (Wu et al.,2016) with tuned (\alpha) on a held-out validation set.
 6 Graph construction overhead. Static analysis for data-flow and call-graph
   extraction adds preprocessing time. For large repositories (10k+ LOC per
   file), parsing and graph construction may become a bottleneck. Mitigation:
   measure and report end-to-end inference latency including graph construction,
   and propose incremental graph update strategies if the overhead is
   prohibitive.

LimitationsLanguage scope. This work targets Java (primary) and Python
(secondary). Java's static type system makes data-flow extraction more reliable,
while Python's dynamic features (duck typing, monkey-patching) introduce
imprecision in def-use analysis. Performance on dynamically-typed languages may
be lower than on statically-typed languages. Extending to C/C++, JavaScript, or
Rust would require language-specific static analysis frontends but the
architectural principles are language-agnostic.

Single-file assumption. The current graph construction operates within a single
file. Many real-world bugs span files, classes, or modules. Extending to
cross-file graphs (e.g., whole-repository graphs) is a natural next step but
introduces scalability challenges (graphs with100k+ nodes) that are beyond the
scope of this proposal.

No human study. We evaluate repair correctness against test suites and
developer-written patches (Defects4J annotations). However, test suites can be
incomplete, and a patch that passes all tests may still be semantically wrong. A
human evaluation of patch quality (developer acceptance rate,
time-to-understand) is absent. This is a limitation we acknowledge but consider
outside the scope of the current proposal, which focuses on automated benchmark
evaluation.

Dataset bias. Defects4J, HumanEval-Java, and QuixBugs are widely used but do not
represent the full distribution of real-world bugs. Bugs tend to be localized
(1–5 lines changed) and in well-tested code. The model's performance on rare,
complex, or security-critical bugs remains unknown.

Training compute. Fine-tuning a model of size comparable to CodeT5-base (~220M
parameters) with relational graph attention adds approximately15–25% overhead
per training step due to the additional relation-bias computations and graph
batching. Full training requires single-GPU (A10040GB) training for
approximately3–4 days. All experiments report total compute budget to facilitate
reproducibility.

No guarantee of type-correctness in generated patches. While we filter patches
that fail type-checking, the type checker is conservative (rejects some valid
patches, accepts some invalid ones under Java's type inference). The TSR metric
is diagnostic but not a guarantee of semantic correctness.

Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

Table3 – Ablation Variant (-IDE): Complete Research Proposal---

TitleCalibrated Consistency: A Multi-Pass Agreement Framework for Accurate
Automated LLM Evaluation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemAutomated evaluation of LLM outputs using LLM-as-a-judge methods suffers
from systematic inaccuracies: position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement
bias (judges favoring their own outputs), and poor calibration on nuanced
quality dimensions (coherence, factual consistency, instruction following).
Current single-pass scoring or pairwise comparison protocols produce high
variance and low inter-rater reliability compared to human judgments. These
issues compound when automated evaluation is used for model development — noisy
signals lead to suboptimal training decisions and unreliable leaderboard
rankings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA multi-pass agreement framework that aggregates multiple independent
evaluation passes with controlled randomization of prompt order, rubric
decomposition, and judge model diversity will reduce bias and variance,
achieving Pearson/Spearman correlations with human judgments that exceed both
single-pass LLM judges and standard baseline methods. Specifically, decomposing
a single holistic quality score into3–5 factor-specific sub-scores (e.g.,
factuality, coherence, instruction following, verbosity penalty) and aggregating
across (k\geq3) structurally diverse judge models will outperform any
single-judge setup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method### Stage1: Multi-Pass Eval ProtocolFor each (model, prompt, reference
response) triple:

 1 Rubric decomposition – Replace a single holistic score with4 sub-criteria
   scored on a1–5 Likert scale:

 • Factual consistency: Does the output contradict known facts or provided
   context?
 • Instruction fidelity: Does the output follow all constraints in the prompt?
 • Coherence & structure: Is the argument logically ordered and well-formed?
 • Conciseness: Does the output avoid unnecessary verbosity? (penalty for
   over-generation)

 2 Judge model diversity – Use3 structurally different judge models (e.g.,
   Mixtral-8x7B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3-70B) to reduce systematic bias.
 3 Randomized presentation – For each judge model, run2 passes with candidate
   order shuffled (when pairwise) or candidate presentation order randomized
   (when scoring). Aggregate via trimmed mean (discard highest and lowest per
   dimension).
 4 Calibration layer – Fit a linear regression or isotonic regression on a
   held-out human-annotated set (N=500) mapping aggregate judge scores to human
   scores, producing recalibrated final scores per dimension.

Stage2: Consensus ScoringCompute inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha
across the3 judge models ×2 passes =6 judgments per dimension). Flag cases with
alpha <0.4 for manual review. For non-flagged items, use the mean of all6
recalibrated scores. Report both the calibrated score and the agreement
statistic alongside it.

Stage3: Uncertainty ReportingInstead of a single point estimate, report
per-example evaluation results as a tuple: (mean score,95% CI from6 judgments,
agreement α). For benchmark-level metrics, report the distribution of CIs and
the proportion of items exceeding the agreement threshold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / BenchmarkPrimary: MT-Bench (80 multi-turn questions,3.3K human
preference judgments labeled by domain experts on a1–10 scale across6 models).
This is the most widely used benchmark for LLM judge accuracy and provides
published human baselines.

Secondary: Chatbot Arena subset —1,000 curated conversations with human Elo
ratings (released as a public dataset) to test generalization beyond the
MT-Bench format.

Calibration set: A randomly sampled20% of the MT-Bench human annotations (N=660
judgments) will be held out for fitting the calibration regression.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | Spearman ρ (primary) | Rank-order correlation with human scores;
captures whether the evaluator preserves relative ordering | | Pearson r |
Linear correlation with human scores; captures absolute agreement | |
Krippendorff's α | Inter-judge reliability among the6 judge passes (ordinal
weighting) | | Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration error after
recalibration — how well do predicted scores match human score distribution? | |
Flag rate | Proportion of items with α <0.4 requiring manual review (lower is
better; controlled human cost) |

All metrics reported with bootstrap95% CIs (10,000 resamples).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. LLM-only single-pass (GPT-4) — Standard single LLM judge with no
rubric, no randomization (state-of-the-art baseline).

 2 Pairwise Elo — Bradley-Terry Elo computed from pairwise comparisons (Chatbot
   Arena protocol, single judge model).
 3 Rubric-only — Single judge model with rubric decomposition but no multi-pass
   aggregation.
 4 Multi-pass single model —6 passes (2× with randomized order) from one judge
   model, no diversity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations (within the proposed method)


 Ablation      What it tests
 -MultiJudge   Drop diversity: use only GPT-4o-mini for all6 passes
 -Calibration  Remove the held-out regression layer
 -Rubric       Replace decomposed sub-scores with a single holistic score
 -AgreeFilter  Remove the α <0.4 flag-and-review step; use all items
 k=2 passes    Reduce from2 to1 pass per model (3 judges ×1 pass =3 judgments
               total)


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Calibration overfitting — The regression layer may
overfit to the specific distribution of MT-Bench human scores, failing to
generalize to the Chatbot Arena subset. Mitigation: evaluate cross-benchmark
transfer and report per-benchmark performance separately.

 2 Diminishing returns on judge count — Three structurally diverse judges may
   not be enough; five may be needed for stable agreement thresholds.
   Mitigation: include an exploratory analysis using5 judges on a subset (200
   items) to confirm the saturation point.
 3 Rubric overspecification — Decomposing into4 sub-scores may miss emergent
   quality dimensions (e.g., creativity, safety) that humans consider
   holistically. Mitigation: include an open-ended "overall impression"
   sub-score as a fifth dimension and compare against the4-factor version.
 4 Agreement filter bias — Items with low inter-judge agreement (α <0.4) may be
   systematically harder or more ambiguous cases, not just noise. Excluding them
   inflates apparent accuracy. Mitigation: report results both with and without
   flagged items; analyze the flagged subset qualitatively.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations1. Judge model access — GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3-70B are accessible
now, but closed-source judge models create reproducibility dependencies. The
Mixtral-8x7B component is fully open-weight and replicable.

 2 Benchmark coverage — MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena cover instruction-following
   and conversation quality but not domain-specific evaluation (medical, legal,
   code generation). The method's generality to specialized domains is untested.
 3 Calibration cost — The calibration set requires500+ human annotations per new
   benchmark, which may be prohibitive for rapid prototyping. Active learning or
   few-shot calibration is left for future work.
 4 Throughput —6 LLM API calls per evaluated item ×4 sub-scores increases
   evaluation cost by6× over a single-pass judge. The trade-off between cost and
   accuracy is characterized but not optimized.
 5 No meta-evaluation — This proposal evaluates the evaluator against human
   judgments, but does not address whether improved evaluation fidelity
   translates into better downstream model training (e.g., RLHF reward signal
   quality). That is a separate evaluation loop not covered here.

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations
Each ablation removes or varies one component of CEE while holding
everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates
Panel size               K =1 vs3 vs5 models        Value of model diversity
Criterion decomposition  Replace6 criteria with     Value of atomic rubric
single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment
Uncertainty weighting    Replace                    Value of log-prob
confidence-weighted        confidence signal
average with uniform
average
Calibration layer        Remove calibration (use    Value of human-anchored
raw aggregated scores)     calibration
Model diversity          Same-family panel (GPT-4o  Value of cross-family
×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated
(GPT-4o + Claude + Llama)  sampling

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is
poorly calibrated — score-token log-probs may not reflect true judgment
confidence, especially under sampling temperature >0 | Medium | Set temperature
to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with
self-reported confidence ("How confident are you in this score on a1-5 scale?")
as an alternative confidence signal |
